question: Under F.A.C. 61J2-14.008(3), the term 'immediately' as it applies to a broker's deposit of escrowed funds means:
choice_a: No later than the end of the third business day following receipt of the item to be deposited
choice_b: Within one calendar hour of receipt
choice_c: Within 30 calendar days of receipt
choice_d: At closing only, with no earlier deadline
explanation: F.A.C. 61J2-14.008(3) defines 'immediately' as placement of a deposit in the escrow account no later than the end of the third business day following receipt of the item to be deposited, excluding Saturdays, Sundays, and legal holidays from the business-day count.

question: A sales associate who personally receives an earnest money deposit from a buyer must deliver it to their broker no later than:
choice_a: The end of the third business day following receipt
choice_b: The end of the next business day following receipt
choice_c: Within 30 calendar days
choice_d: At the closing table only
explanation: F.A.C. 61J2-14.009 requires a sales associate or broker associate who receives escrow funds to deliver them to the broker no later than the end of the next business day following receipt; the broker then has until the end of the third business day following receipt to place the funds in the escrow account under 61J2-14.010(1).

question: Combining the sales associate delivery rule and the broker deposit rule, the maximum total time from a sales associate's receipt of an earnest money check to the broker's deposit of it into the escrow account is generally:
choice_a: The associate must personally deposit the funds within 1 hour of receipt, bypassing the broker entirely
choice_b: There is no time limit as long as the funds are deposited before closing
choice_c: The associate has 1 business day to deliver to the broker, and the broker then has up to 3 business days from its own receipt to deposit -- meaning the funds can sit up to about 3 business days after the broker actually receives them
choice_d: The combined deadline is always exactly 24 hours regardless of who receives the funds first
explanation: F.A.C. 61J2-14.009 and 61J2-14.010(1)/61J2-14.008(3) work together: a sales associate must hand off funds to the broker by the end of the next business day, and the broker's own 3-business-day 'immediately' deposit clock runs from the broker's own receipt of the funds, not the associate's.

question: Where may a Florida broker properly maintain an escrow account for holding trust funds received in a real estate transaction?
choice_a: The broker's personal home safe only
choice_b: A cryptocurrency wallet controlled solely by the broker
choice_c: Any out-of-state financial institution with no Florida presence
choice_d: A bank, savings and loan association, trust company, credit union, or title company having trust powers
explanation: A Florida broker must place trust funds in an insured escrow or trust account at a bank, savings and loan association, trust company, credit union, or title company having trust powers -- a properly regulated depository, not the broker's personal possession.

question: If a broker has a good faith doubt as to which party is entitled to trust funds held in the broker's escrow account, the broker must provide written notification to FREC within how many business days of having that doubt?
choice_a: 15 business days
choice_b: 5 business days
choice_c: 45 business days
choice_d: 90 business days
explanation: F.A.C. 61J2-10.032 requires a broker who has a good faith doubt about entitlement to escrowed funds to provide written notification to the Florida Real Estate Commission within 15 business days of having that doubt.

question: Upon receiving conflicting demands for trust funds held in the broker's escrow account, a broker must notify FREC in writing within how many business days of the last party's demand?
choice_a: 60 business days
choice_b: 15 business days
choice_c: 3 business days
choice_d: There is no deadline as long as the funds remain in escrow
explanation: Just as with a good faith doubt, F.A.C. 61J2-10.032 requires a broker who receives conflicting demands for escrowed trust funds to notify FREC in writing within 15 business days of the date of the last conflicting demand.

question: After notifying FREC of a good faith doubt or conflicting demands over escrowed funds, a broker must institute one of the settlement procedures under Section 475.25(1)(d)1., F.S., within how many business days?
choice_a: 5 business days
choice_b: 180 business days
choice_c: 30 business days after the last demand or after having the doubt
choice_d: There is no deadline to institute a settlement procedure
explanation: A broker must institute one of the statutory settlement procedures -- requesting an escrow disbursement order (EDO), submitting to arbitration, submitting to mediation, or filing an interpleader action -- within 30 business days after the last demand or after the broker's own good faith doubt arose.

question: Which of the following is NOT one of the statutory settlement procedures a broker may use to resolve a dispute over escrowed funds under Section 475.25(1)(d)1., F.S.?
choice_a: Requesting an escrow disbursement order (EDO) from FREC
choice_b: Submitting the dispute to arbitration, with consent of the parties
choice_c: Filing an interpleader action in court
choice_d: Unilaterally disbursing the funds to whichever party the broker personally believes is entitled
explanation: A broker may never unilaterally disburse disputed escrowed funds based on their own personal judgment; the statutory settlement procedures are an escrow disbursement order (EDO) from FREC, consensual arbitration, consensual mediation, or a judicial interpleader action -- unilateral disbursement is expressly what these procedures exist to prevent.

question: If a broker and the disputing parties agree to submit an escrow dispute to mediation, that mediation must generally conclude within how long following the last demand, or the broker must pursue an alternate settlement procedure?
choice_a: 90 days
choice_b: 10 days
choice_c: 1 year
choice_d: There is no time limit on mediation
explanation: When a broker elects mediation as the settlement procedure for a disputed escrow claim, the mediation must generally conclude within 90 days following the last demand; if it does not, the broker must pursue one of the other settlement procedures instead of leaving the matter unresolved indefinitely.

question: A broker who deposits personal operating funds into the same escrow account holding client trust money, even briefly, has most likely committed:
choice_a: A permissible accounting shortcut as long as it is reconciled later
choice_b: Commingling, a serious violation regardless of intent or ultimate harm
choice_c: A minor bookkeeping issue with no regulatory significance
choice_d: A required step to keep the escrow account properly funded
explanation: Commingling personal or brokerage operating funds with client trust money is expressly prohibited under Section 475.25(1)(k), F.S., and is treated as a serious violation regardless of whether any client was actually harmed or whether the broker intended to correct it later.
source_note: Section 475.25(1)(k), F.S. (immediate escrow placement / commingling prohibition)

question: Which of the following grounds for discipline under Section 475.25(1)(b), F.S., specifically covers a broker's mishandling of client trust funds through dishonesty or gross carelessness?
choice_a: Failure to renew a license on time
choice_b: Advertising without including the brokerage's phone number
choice_c: Fraud, misrepresentation, concealment, false promises, false pretenses, dishonest dealing by trick, scheme, or device, culpable negligence, or breach of trust
choice_d: Failing to attend a mandatory continuing education seminar
explanation: Section 475.25(1)(b), F.S., is the broad discipline provision covering fraud, misrepresentation, concealment, false promises or pretenses, dishonest dealing by trick, scheme, or device, culpable negligence, or breach of trust -- language regularly applied to serious trust account misconduct.

question: A broker's failure to properly account for or deliver trust funds to the person entitled to them, absent a legitimate good faith dispute, constitutes a violation of:
choice_a: Section 475.278, F.S. (brokerage relationships)
choice_b: Section 475.611, F.S.
choice_c: Chapter 720, F.S.
choice_d: Section 475.25(1)(d)1., F.S. (failure to account and deliver)
explanation: Section 475.25(1)(d)1., F.S., makes it a disciplinable offense for a licensee to fail to account or deliver to any person entitled to it any money, fund, deposit, or other property that has come into the licensee's hands -- the core failure-to-account provision underlying most escrow discipline cases.

question: A broker's escrow account must be reconciled how often, per F.A.C. 61J2-14.012's minimum recordkeeping expectations?
choice_a: Monthly, with a written reconciliation statement reviewed, signed, and dated by the broker
choice_b: Only once, when the account is first opened
choice_c: Annually, at license renewal time
choice_d: Only when a specific client complaint is filed
explanation: F.A.C. 61J2-14.012 requires a monthly written reconciliation of the broker's escrow account; while an accountant or bookkeeper may prepare the statement, the broker must review, sign, and date it, since the broker remains ultimately responsible for the funds.

question: Under F.A.C. 61J2-14.012, a broker's monthly escrow reconciliation statement must at minimum include which of the following?
choice_a: Only the total dollar amount currently in the account, with no supporting detail
choice_b: The bank name, account name and number, account balance and date, deposits in transit, outstanding checks by date and number, and an itemized list of the broker's total trust liability
choice_c: The broker's personal net worth statement
choice_d: A list of every sales associate's home address
explanation: F.A.C. 61J2-14.012 specifies detailed minimum content for the monthly reconciliation: reconciliation date, balance date, bank and account identifying information, account balance, deposits in transit, outstanding checks identified by date and number, and an itemized list of the broker's trust liability -- sufficient detail to independently verify the account matches what is actually owed to clients.

question: If a broker's monthly escrow reconciliation reveals that the trust liability and the bank balance do not agree, F.A.C. 61J2-14.012 requires the broker to:
choice_a: Ignore the discrepancy as long as it is under $100
choice_b: Immediately close the account with no further documentation
choice_c: Include a description or explanation of the difference and any corrective action taken
choice_d: Wait for the next annual audit before addressing it
explanation: Whenever a reconciliation reveals a discrepancy between the trust liability and the bank balance, the broker's reconciliation record must describe or explain the difference and document any corrective action taken -- a discrepancy left unexplained is itself a red flag for a shortage or misappropriation.

question: A broker discovers an unexplained shortage in the firm's escrow account upon reviewing bank statements. The broker's legal and ethical obligation is to:
choice_a: Wait until the next scheduled FREC audit to address it
choice_b: Quietly transfer personal funds to cover it with no further investigation or documentation
choice_c: Assume it is a bank error and take no action
choice_d: Investigate immediately, correct the shortage, and treat it as a serious compliance matter, since an unresolved shortage indicates client funds may be missing
explanation: An escrow shortage requires immediate investigation and correction, because it signals that client funds may be missing, misapplied, or improperly disbursed; failing to investigate and document the cause fails to address the underlying compliance failure and can compound the broker's liability.

question: In a residential sale, the parties may agree that earnest money be held not by the listing broker, but by a title company or attorney serving as escrow agent. In that case:
choice_a: The title company or attorney -- not the broker -- assumes escrow-holder responsibilities for those funds, per the transaction's agreed escrow arrangement
choice_b: The broker must still personally hold a duplicate set of the same funds
choice_c: This arrangement is never permitted under Florida law
choice_d: The broker remains the only party who may ever disburse the funds
explanation: Florida real estate contracts commonly designate a title company or closing attorney as escrow agent instead of the broker; when the parties' agreement does so, escrow-holder responsibilities for those funds shift to that designated agent rather than the broker.
source_note: DBPR Real Estate Broker Candidate Information Booklet, Content Overview and Outline, Section I.D.9 (Title Company and Attorney Held)

question: A broker managing rental properties who collects tenants' security deposits and advance rent must handle those funds:
choice_a: Under no regulatory framework at all, since rental funds are exempt from escrow rules
choice_b: Under the same trust/escrow account rules that apply to sales earnest money, since they are also trust funds held on behalf of another
choice_c: By depositing them directly into the property owner's personal account with no broker involvement
choice_d: By holding the funds in cash in the office safe indefinitely
explanation: Security deposits and advance rent collected by a property-managing broker constitute trust funds and are subject to the same deposit-timing, recordkeeping, and non-commingling rules that govern sales earnest money, since the broker holds them in a fiduciary capacity on behalf of another.
source_note: F.A.C. 61J2-14.010; DBPR Real Estate Broker Candidate Information Booklet, Content Overview and Outline, Section I.D.11 (Property Management Deposits and Advance Rent)

question: A broker holding property management trust funds for multiple rental property owners in a single pooled escrow account must maintain records sufficient to:
choice_a: Track only the aggregate account balance, with no owner-level detail required
choice_b: Avoid any recordkeeping as long as the account never runs a deficit
choice_c: Reconcile the account and account separately for each owner's funds within the pooled account
choice_d: Report solely to the tenants, not the property owners
explanation: Even where a broker pools multiple owners' funds into a single designated trust account, the broker must maintain individual ledgers allowing each owner's funds to be reconciled separately, consistent with F.A.C. 61J2-14.012's reconciliation requirements and general fiduciary recordkeeping duties for property management trust funds.
source_note: F.A.C. 61J2-14.012; general property management trust accounting practice

question: A broker's use of trust account funds to cover the brokerage's own operating expenses, such as office rent or a sales associate's commission draw, before those funds are properly earned and disbursed is:
choice_a: Permissible as long as the broker replaces the funds before month-end
choice_b: Standard industry practice with no compliance risk
choice_c: Permitted only for brokers with more than 10 years of experience
choice_d: A clear commingling and misappropriation violation
explanation: An escrow/trust account exists solely to hold funds belonging to others in a fiduciary capacity; using it to pay the brokerage's own operating expenses or commission advances is a clear commingling and misappropriation violation, regardless of whether the broker intends to reimburse the account later.

question: Interest earned on funds held in a broker's interest-bearing escrow account under F.A.C. 61J2-14.014 is generally:
choice_a: Governed by the terms of the parties' written agreement as to who is entitled to the interest
choice_b: Always retained by the broker as compensation for managing the account
choice_c: Always forfeited to the State of Florida
choice_d: Split automatically 50/50 between buyer and seller with no agreement needed
explanation: F.A.C. 61J2-14.014 addresses interest-bearing escrow accounts, but entitlement to any interest earned is governed by the parties' written agreement (e.g., a contract provision directing interest to a particular party, a charity, or the broker for administrative costs, if disclosed and agreed) rather than being automatically retained by the broker.

question: A condominium association's property manager broker handling reserve funds and special assessments collected from unit owners must generally treat those funds as:
choice_a: The association's discretionary general revenue with no fiduciary constraints
choice_b: Trust funds subject to fiduciary handling and recordkeeping requirements similar to other client funds
choice_c: Funds exempt from any trust account rules because condominiums are governed exclusively by Chapter 718
choice_d: Funds the broker may use interchangeably with the brokerage's operating account
explanation: Reserve funds and special assessments collected on behalf of a condominium association are held in a fiduciary capacity and generally remain subject to trust-fund handling principles even though Chapter 718, F.S. (Condominiums) also imposes its own separate association-level financial requirements.
source_note: Chapter 718, F.S. (Condominiums); DBPR Real Estate Broker Candidate Information Booklet, Content Overview and Outline, Section I.D.12

question: Florida real estate brokers agreeing to fix commission rates collectively with competing brokerages would most directly risk violating:
choice_a: Escrow account rules, since commission rates have no antitrust dimension
choice_b: Fair Housing law exclusively
choice_c: Antitrust law, since price-fixing among competing brokerages is prohibited
choice_d: Nothing, since commission rates are fully regulated by FREC and set by rule
explanation: Real estate commission rates are freely negotiable in Florida, and brokers agreeing with competitors to fix or standardize commission rates would violate federal and state antitrust law (e.g., Sherman Act Section 1; Chapter 542, F.S.) -- FREC does not set or regulate commission rates.
source_note: Chapter 542, F.S. (Combinations Restricting Trade or Commerce); DBPR Real Estate Broker Candidate Information Booklet, Content Overview and Outline, Section I.D.10.a

question: Florida's Commercial Real Estate Sales Commission Lien Act allows a broker owed an unpaid commission on a commercial transaction to claim a lien against:
choice_a: The real property title directly, in the same manner as a mechanic's lien
choice_b: The buyer's personal assets unrelated to the transaction
choice_c: Nothing; brokers have no statutory lien remedy in Florida
choice_d: The owner's net sale proceeds -- not the real property itself
explanation: Chapter 475, Part III, F.S. (Sections 475.700-475.719, the Commercial Real Estate Sales Commission Lien Act) allows a broker to claim a statutory lien to secure payment of an earned commission, but that lien attaches to the owner's net sale proceeds -- not to the commercial real property's title itself.
source_note: Sections 475.700-475.719, F.S. (Commercial Real Estate Sales Commission Lien Act)

question: The Florida Commercial Real Estate Leasing Commission Lien Act, addressing a broker's commission lien remedy for lease transactions, is codified separately at:
choice_a: Chapter 475, Part IV, F.S.
choice_b: Chapter 475, Part I, F.S.
choice_c: Chapter 83, F.S. exclusively
choice_d: Chapter 720, F.S.
explanation: Florida provides a parallel commission-lien remedy specifically for commercial leasing transactions under Chapter 475, Part IV, F.S. (the Commercial Real Estate Leasing Commission Lien Act), distinct from Part III's sales-transaction lien act.
source_note: Chapter 475, Part IV, F.S. (Commercial Real Estate Leasing Commission Lien Act)

question: A broker who receives a purchase contract deposit made payable directly to a title company, rather than to the broker, generally:
choice_a: Must always deposit every check into the broker's own escrow account regardless of payee
choice_b: May deliver the check to the authorized title company/escrow agent rather than deposit it into the broker's own escrow account, consistent with the transaction's agreed escrow arrangement
choice_c: May keep the check indefinitely without delivering it anywhere
choice_d: Must return the check to the buyer and refuse to proceed
explanation: When the transaction's agreement designates a title company as escrow agent, a broker who receives a check made payable to that title company may properly deliver it there rather than deposit it into the broker's own escrow account -- a common and accepted practice in Florida residential closings.
source_note: F.A.C. 61J2-14.010; DBPR Real Estate Broker Candidate Information Booklet, Content Overview and Outline, Section I.D.9

question: A broker's failure to maintain trust account records for the period required, discovered during a random FREC audit even without a pending client complaint, can still result in:
choice_a: No consequence unless a specific client complaint is also filed
choice_b: Automatic dismissal of the audit, since FREC lacks authority to audit absent a complaint
choice_c: FREC disciplinary action for the recordkeeping violation itself
choice_d: A private civil lawsuit only, with FREC having no independent jurisdiction
explanation: FREC and DBPR's Bureau of Enforcement have independent authority to audit broker escrow accounts and pursue discipline for recordkeeping violations discovered during that audit, separate from and regardless of whether any specific consumer complaint has been filed.
source_note: F.A.C. 61J2-14.012; DBPR Division of Real Estate Bureau of Enforcement guidance

question: A broker found guilty of misappropriating escrow funds faces which range of disciplinary penalties under Section 475.25, F.S.?
choice_a: Only a verbal warning, with no formal penalty structure
choice_b: A mandatory criminal prison sentence with no administrative option
choice_c: Automatic permanent revocation with no other penalty ever available
choice_d: An administrative fine up to $5,000 per count, license suspension of up to 10 years, revocation, probation, or reprimand
explanation: Section 475.25, F.S., authorizes a range of disciplinary penalties for licensees found in violation, including an administrative fine not to exceed $5,000 per count or separate offense, suspension of up to 10 years, revocation, probation, and reprimand -- with escrow misappropriation typically treated toward the severe end of that range.

question: The Florida Real Estate Recovery Fund exists to:
choice_a: Compensate individuals who suffer monetary losses due to the fraudulent, deceptive, or negligent acts of a licensed broker or sales associate, up to statutory caps
choice_b: Reimburse brokers for their own business losses
choice_c: Pay FREC's administrative operating budget
choice_d: Fund advertising campaigns promoting the real estate profession
explanation: The Real Estate Recovery Fund, established under Section 475.482, F.S., compensates consumers who suffer monetary losses from a licensee's fraudulent, deceptive, or negligent conduct and who cannot otherwise collect a judgment -- it is a consumer-protection fund, not a benefit for licensees themselves.

question: Under Section 475.484, F.S., a single Recovery Fund claimant's payment for actual/compensatory damages from one licensee is capped at:
choice_a: $5,000 flat, regardless of the judgment amount
choice_b: $50,000, or the unsatisfied portion of the judgment, whichever is less
choice_c: $1,000,000 per claimant
choice_d: There is no per-claimant cap
explanation: Section 475.484, F.S., caps a single Recovery Fund claimant's recovery at $50,000 or the unsatisfied portion of the claimant's judgment, whichever is less -- with an aggregate transaction cap of $50,000 across all claimants/properties in the same transaction.

question: Under Section 475.484, F.S., total Recovery Fund payments arising from claims against any single broker or sales associate are capped in the aggregate at:
choice_d: There is no aggregate per-licensee cap
explanation: Section 475.484, F.S., caps aggregate Recovery Fund payments attributable to claims against any single licensee at $150,000, regardless of how many individual claimants or transactions are involved.
source_note: Section 475.484, F.S. (Recovery Fund per-licensee aggregate limit)

question: The Real Estate Recovery Fund is funded in part by a per-license annual fee added to the renewal cost; brokers currently contribute at what per-year rate toward the fund, as long as fund collection has not been suspended?
choice_a: $50 per year for brokers
choice_b: Nothing -- the fund is financed solely through general tax revenue
choice_c: $500 per year for brokers
choice_d: $3.50 per year for brokers ($1.50 per year for sales associates)
explanation: A statutory Recovery Fund fee of $3.50 per year is added to a broker's license fee ($1.50 per year for sales associates); collection is suspended once the fund exceeds $1 million and does not resume unless the fund balance falls below $500,000.
